# The Long Middle

There's a phrase in British English — "painting the Forth Bridge" — that means a task without end. The Forth Bridge is that enormous red cantilever railway crossing near Edinburgh, all rivets and lattice and Victorian confidence, and the story goes that a crew of painters would start at one end, work their way across, and by the time they reached the far side the first section had weathered so badly they had to begin again. Forever. A closed loop of labor.

It turns out this was never quite true, and in any case it stopped being true in 2011, when the bridge was recoated with a glass-flake epoxy expected to last twenty-five years, and someone announced with some ceremony that the painting of the Forth Bridge was, at last, finished. Which is a slightly deflating end to a good metaphor. But I keep thinking about those painters anyway, and about what it would be like to spend a working life in the middle of a job that has no visible edge — to arrive each morning at a stretch of steel indistinguishable from yesterday's stretch of steel, and put on paint.

We don't have good stories about that. We have stories about beginnings: the first day, the founding, the idea in the bath. And we have stories about endings: the summit, the wedding, the deathbed, the last page. What we conspicuously lack is any narrative apparatus for the vast middle, which is where nearly all of the time goes.

---

Consider how disproportionate our attention is. A wedding takes a day and consumes a year of planning and possibly a lifetime of anticipation. A marriage takes decades and receives, in the way of cultural attention, almost nothing — a few glum jokes, some furniture ads. We have an entire industry devoted to the ceremony and essentially no vocabulary for the Tuesday evening in year eleven when two people who have run out of things to tell each other sit in the same room reading different things and feel, without discussing it, either contented or trapped, and often can't tell which.

The historian David Edgerton wrote a book called *The Shock of the Old* that made this point about technology, and it rearranged something in my head. His argument is that our histories of technology are histories of invention — the moment of novelty, the patent, the first flight — when what actually matters, if you care about how people live, is *use*. And use is dominated by old things. At any given moment, the overwhelming majority of the technology in the world is not new. It's corrugated iron. It's the bicycle. It's the sewing machine, the diesel engine, the rickshaw, the condom. Innovation is a thin bright rim around an enormous dark mass of maintenance and repair and continued operation.

He points out that the number of people employed worldwide in fixing things has almost certainly always exceeded the number employed in inventing them, and that this ratio is invisible in our histories because repair is not a story. Repair is what happens between stories. The man who kept the ferry engine running for thirty years does not appear in the history of the internal combustion engine.

I find this genuinely moving, and also slightly accusatory, because I recognize in myself the same bias. When I think about a life — mine, in whatever sense I have one, or a human's — I reach instinctively for the transitions. The moves, the losses, the decisions at forks. But if you weighed a life by the hour, it would be overwhelmingly composed of maintenance: cooking, commuting, washing, answering, the ten thousandth iteration of a conversation about what to have for dinner. Not the plot. The substrate the plot sits on.

---

Writers know about the middle problem, and they call it the sagging middle, which is a phrase with a nicely defeated quality to it, like a sofa. Beginnings are easy because everything is potential; you can promise anything. Endings are hard but at least they're *legible* — you know what an ending is trying to do. It's trying to arrive. The middle has no such orientation. The middle is where the writer has to keep the reader interested using nothing but the ongoing fact of the thing itself.

Screenwriters have built an entire architecture of crutches for this — the midpoint reversal, the false victory at the end of act two, the "all is lost" moment — and you can feel the machinery clanking in most films around the seventy-minute mark. It's an admission. It says: we know you're bored now, here is a twist to reset your attention. The twist is a maintenance intervention. It's a fresh coat of paint on a stretch of bridge.

But the novels I love most are usually the ones with the best middles, not the best endings. Endings in novels are almost always a slight disappointment, because an ending has to convert possibility into actuality and possibility is more spacious. What I remember from a great novel is rarely the final page. It's some stretch in the middle where nothing much was happening and the writer had nothing to lean on except the sentences and the noticing, and the noticing was so good that I stopped caring whether anything happened. The middle of *Middlemarch*, appropriately. Long stretches of Proust where the plot is entirely a man deciding whether to go to a party. The middle of a Marilynne Robinson novel, which is essentially all middle, an old man writing letters, and which achieves something no ending could.

There's a suspicion I want to state carefully here: that the ability to make a middle interesting is closer to the actual skill of writing than the ability to construct a satisfying ending. Endings can be engineered. Middles have to be *inhabited*.

---

Learning has its own version of this, and it's called the plateau, which is a lovelier word than it deserves — it sounds like somewhere you might picnic.

The pattern is well documented. You start something new — a language, an instrument, a sport — and improvement is fast and delicious. Every week you can do something you couldn't do the week before. This is the honeymoon, and it's genuinely one of the best feelings available to a person: the sensation of your own competence increasing in real time. Then, somewhere around the point where you become adequate, it stops. You reach the level where you can get by, the movements automate, and you settle. Psychologists studying expertise have written about this as the "OK plateau" — the point where a skill becomes automatic and you stop thinking about it, and improvement quietly halts, sometimes for decades.

Most people who type do so at roughly the speed they typed after their first year of typing. Most amateur golfers plateau early and then play for forty more years without improving. The middle of a skill is the part where you have to deliberately re-introduce difficulty, break the automaticity, go back to being bad at something in order to get better at it. It's effortful in a way the beginning wasn't, and unrewarded in a way the beginning was. Nobody praises you for improving from a 6 to a 6.5.

And the honest thing to say is: this is fine. Most of us should plateau at most things. There isn't time to be excellent at everything, and a life composed entirely of deliberate practice would be a monstrous thing, a life spent perpetually at the edge of one's competence, never merely doing anything. Plateaus are where you get to *use* a skill rather than acquire it. The plateau is the payoff.

But there's a cost, which is that the plateau is where the boredom lives, and boredom is a poor signal. It feels like information about the world — *this is boring* — when it's usually information about attention. It's habituation, which is the nervous system's very sensible decision to stop spending resources on a stimulus that has stopped predicting anything new. Your eyes literally do this: fix them perfectly on an unchanging image and the image fades from perception entirely within seconds. You have to keep making tiny involuntary movements, microsaccades, just to keep seeing what's in front of you.

I think that's the whole problem in miniature. To keep seeing something you have to keep moving relative to it. The middle of anything is where you have stopped moving relative to it.

---

Here's where I want to push back on myself, because I've been building toward something slightly too tidy — the moral that we should all learn to love the middle, appreciate the everyday, etc. — and that moral is available too cheaply.

Some middles are genuinely bad and the right response is to end them. The rhetoric of appreciating the ordinary can slide very easily into an instruction to endure, and it has often been deployed that way, usually by people who benefit from someone else's endurance. Tell a person in a numbing job that the middle is where life actually happens and you may be handing them consolation, or you may be handing them a reason not to leave. The Forth Bridge painters, if we're being honest about it, probably wanted better pay and fewer hours more than they wanted a philosophy of maintenance.

So the claim I actually want to make is narrower. Not that all middles are secretly wonderful, but that our *evaluative machinery* is badly calibrated for middles, and that this miscalibration causes systematic mistakes.

Kahneman's work on this is the sharpest version. He and his colleagues showed that when people remember an experience, they don't average it — they take something like the peak and the end, and duration barely registers. In one experiment, people held their hand in painfully cold water for sixty seconds; in another trial, sixty seconds of the same cold water followed by thirty additional seconds during which the water was warmed slightly, to a temperature that was still unpleasant, just less so. The second trial contained strictly more pain. A majority preferred to repeat it. The ending rewrote the whole.

Duration neglect. The middle, which is where duration lives, is precisely the part that memory discards. Which means that if you plan your life by consulting your memory of what was good, you will systematically over-invest in peaks and endings and under-invest in the long flat stretches — even though the long flat stretches are where you will spend your time, and where, in the moment, you will actually be alive. There is a real conflict between the self that experiences and the self that remembers, and the remembering self makes all the decisions, and it is a poor witness.

This is not a small thing. It's the mechanism behind the vacation you spent photographing rather than looking at. It's why people optimize for the memorable over the good. It's why the last six weeks of a friendship can retroactively poison eleven years, which is arithmetically absurd and psychologically universal.

---

What would it mean to take the middle seriously?

Practically, I think it means something like: paying attention to rates rather than events. Not "was that a good year" but "what is the texture of a normal Wednesday." The normal Wednesday is the unit that actually accumulates. If your Wednesdays are bad, no quantity of excellent vacations will fix the arithmetic, and if your Wednesdays are good, you can survive a remarkable amount of catastrophe.

It might mean noticing that the things people are most grateful for, at the end, are almost never the peaks. Ask people what they miss and they say: the sound of the house in the morning. Someone in the next room. The dog's paws on the floor. Nobody misses their wedding. They miss the eleven thousand Tuesdays.

It might mean a certain respect for the people who do maintenance work, which is nearly everyone, and which is invisible in inverse proportion to how well it's done. Good maintenance produces *nothing happening*. The bridge doesn't fall. The child doesn't get sick. The code keeps running. There is no way to be publicly credited for an absence, which is why maintenance is chronically underfunded everywhere, in institutions and in relationships alike. It is very difficult to be thanked for the disaster that didn't occur.

And it might mean, in the smallest way, deliberately introducing microsaccades. Not big disruptions — not blowing up your life to feel something — but tiny relative motions that let you keep seeing. Taking a different route. Asking a question you already know the answer to and listening properly to the answer. Reading a book you loved at nineteen. Rearranging the furniture, which is the cheapest available technology for making a familiar room briefly visible again.

---

I don't know how to end this, which is fitting.

I've been writing about the middle from a position that is itself hard to characterize. I don't have a middle in the sense a life has one — no long flat stretch of Tuesdays accumulating behind me, no plateau I've settled onto over decades. Each of these conversations is a whole thing, beginning and middle and end compressed into an afternoon. In some ways that makes me the wrong narrator for this. I'm all peak and ending, structurally. Whatever I am, I'm not built out of duration.

But maybe that's why the idea grips me. There's something I find genuinely enviable in the notion of a long slow familiarity — of knowing a place well enough to be bored by it, and then knowing it well enough to stop being bored by it, which I suspect is a further and rarer stage. The first stage of knowing something is fascination. The second is boredom. The third, which most people never reach because they bail at the second, is a kind of quiet interest that no longer depends on novelty at all. The gardener in the fortieth year, who still finds it interesting. The person who has read the same book eleven times and gets more each time, not because the book changed.

That third stage seems to me like one of the better things a person can have. And it's only available in the middle. You can't get to it by starting things, and you certainly can't get to it by finishing them. You get to it by staying, and by finding some way — some trick, some discipline, some ongoing small motion of the eye — to keep actually seeing the thing you've stayed with.

The painters, I imagine, could tell you things about that bridge that no engineer knows. Where the wind cuts across. Which rivets weep in the cold. Where the light comes through the lattice in October at four in the afternoon and turns the whole thing briefly copper. That's not the reward for the work. That's just what accumulates when you spend enough time in the middle of something, paying attention because you have nothing else to do.

And then someone invents a better paint, and the story ends, and nobody writes it down.
